title: Diffusion-driven autocatalytic dynamics on a sphere
abstract: We study the collective dynamics of independent particles that diffuse outside a spherical surface, on which they are replicated with a prescribed catalytic rate. In spatial dimensions three and higher, the transient nature of diffusion creates the competition between autocatalytic and escape events, thus leading to a rich phase diagram between subcritical (extinction), critical (steady-state), and supercritical (growth) regimes at long times. The rotational symmetry of the domain and an explicit form of the single-particle diffusion propagator allow us to obtain the statistics of the population size (i.e., the number of particles). In this way, we analyze the mean population size, its variance and higher-order moments, as well as the full distribution. In particular, we obtain a fully explicit form of the distribution at long times and describe a slow, power-law approach to this steady-state limit.
summary: This work analyzes autocatalytic dynamics where particles diffuse outside a sphere while replicating upon reaching the boundary. The competition between diffusion escape and self-catalysis leads to three distinct long-time regimes: extinction, steady-state maintenance, or explosive growth. By solving moment equations using advanced mathematical techniques like Laplace transforms, the authors characterize the precise scaling laws governing these transitions.
main_problem: The study investigates the collective dynamics of independent particles diffusing outside a spherical surface where they undergo autocatalytic replication at a prescribed rate.
main_result: The system exhibits three distinct long-time regimes (subcritical, critical, supercritical) characterized by different behaviors for population moments and mean size, including power-law or exponential growth/decay.
method: The analysis uses generating functions and integral equations to track the time evolution of population moments and probability distributions. Asymptotic behavior is determined using Laplace transforms in the long-time limit.
model_or_system: The model describes diffusion in an exterior domain (outside a ball) with autocatalytic reactions occurring on the boundary surface ($\partial\Omega$). The dynamics are governed by the competition between particle escape to infinity and local branching/replication events.
key_observables: Mean population size $\langle N(t) angle$, variance, higher-order moments ($N_k$), and the full probability distribution $Q_k(t)$.
important_parameters: The catalytic rate ($q_c$) relative to a critical value ($q_{crit}$), which determines the system's long-term fate.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes rotational symmetry of the domain (exterior of a ball) and relies on explicit forms for diffusion propagators. The asymptotic results are noted to be expected to hold for generic exterior domains.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the time evolution of population moments ($N_k$) across subcritical, critical, and supercritical regimes, comparing numerical integration against derived asymptotic formulas.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the dynamics via propagators in an unbounded domain to deriving integral equations for moments. It then performs a detailed analysis of the long-time asymptotics by examining different parameter regimes ($q_c$ vs $q_{crit}$) using Laplace transforms.
why_interesting: While focused on classical diffusion and reaction kinetics, the concept of phase transitions (subcritical/critical/supercritical) based on a control parameter ($q_c$) is highly relevant to non-equilibrium statistical mechanics and pattern formation in complex systems.
